blocks.text: This unit closes the work of the module B2.2 and transforms it into a method. In each text there are facts (verifiables), statements (attributed to someone), interpretations (linking facts) and opinions (value judgments). The language signals them with precise markers, but sometimes it confuses them on purpose: "It is evident that """ """"""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""""" In this unit you learn to recognize the markers of each category, to expose opinions disguised as facts, to distinguish established cause and hypothetical cause, and to build a note of analysis in English that separates the four levels. Three weeks, in parallel with ARZ-01 and the beginning of EGY-16.

Targets. At the end of the lesson you know:
1. categorize the sentences of a text in facts, statements, interpretations and opinions, with the markers which the report;
2. recognising the views presented as facts ( ⁧مِنَ الوَاضِحِ أَنَّ⁩ , ⁧الحَقِيقَةُ أَنَّ⁩ , ⁧مِمَّا يَدُلُّ عَلَى أَنَّ⁩ );
3. distinguish a causal relationship established by a proven one;
4. identify what a text does not say (lacune) and what it would take to verify it;
5. write a note of analysis in English with the four separate levels.
